title: America's Wealthiest Aren't CEOs — They Own Car Washes and HVAC Companies
dek: Three million private business owners in the US hold net worths above $5 million, and their combined wealth is more than ten times that of the Forbes 400 — they run car washes, HVAC companies, and auto dealerships, and they got rich by owning, not by earning a salary.
why: The data comes from IRS and Treasury tax records, which are more granular than Federal Reserve surveys. The core conclusion: to reach the top 0.1%, you get there by owning a business, not by earning a high salary.
who: Founders, investors, tax and wealth management professionals who want to understand the real distribution of American wealth and the returns to entrepreneurship.
skip: The discussion of the pandemic and industry disruption from 20:33 to 22:37, which has lower information density.

points.h: The IRS pulled them in to study taxes and they accidentally built a wealth database
points.body: The two authors had just finished graduate school when they were recruited by the Treasury Department and the Office of Tax Analysis to solve a tax policy puzzle: pass-through businesses don't pay taxes themselves, so you have to link the business back to its individual owner to calculate the tax burden. The project accidentally produced a panel database that tracks every business along with its owners and employees — far richer than the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances, which is large in scale but nowhere near as granular as tax records.

points.h: Wealth isn't in Silicon Valley or Wall Street — the whole map lights up
points.body: The authors assumed wealth was concentrated in tech and finance, and the data overturned that bias. When they plotted the "everywhere millionaire" on a map, the entire country lit up. These wealthy people are spread across a large number of unglamorous industries — auto dealerships, HVAC, dental practices, restaurants, distribution, sanitation. It isn't just the Forbes 400 getting richer; it's millions of people getting richer.

points.h: Three million private business owners hold ten times the wealth of the Forbes 400
points.body: The authors counted roughly 3 million "everywhere millionaires" — private business owners with a net worth of at least $5 million. Their combined wealth exceeds the Forbes 400 total by more than ten times. That number changes the inequality narrative: what drives inequality statistics isn't a few hundred billionaires but millions of unknown business owners.

points.h: The higher the income, the smaller the wage share and the larger the business-income share
points.body: Break open the top 10% of earners: people at the 90th percentile rely mainly on wages. But the further up you go, the curves cross — by the top 0.1%, most income comes from business income. The authors say the main typical way to get rich in America is to own something, not to earn a wage. This is both a tax advantage (owning is taxed more lightly than earning a wage) and the actual path of wealth accumulation.

points.h: The 1986 tax reform turned pass-through from a disadvantage into an advantage
points.body: The 1986 tax reform (Reagan as president, Democrats controlling Congress, a bipartisan effort) lowered the individual income tax rate below the corporate rate for the first time. Before that, pass-through status was unattractive because of the tax disadvantage; afterward, being a pass-through became cheaper. Later, the Bush tax cuts lowered individual rates further, and the 2017 tax reform added a 20% deduction for certain pass-through categories. The result: more than half of business income is pass-through income, nearly half of employment is at pass-through businesses, and almost all small businesses are pass-throughs.

points.h: Half of the top 1%'s income growth came from pass-through
points.body: The authors ran a counterfactual: if you held fixed the importance of pass-through business income as it stood in 1985 (before the 1986 tax reform) and let it evolve as it was, roughly half of the top 1%'s income growth would disappear. Looking at wealth growth, from 1989 to the latest SCF data, two-thirds of the top 0.1%'s wealth growth came from private businesses. This shows that pass-through is, in accounting terms, absolutely central to the growth of wealth and top-end income.

points.h: Entrepreneurship pays only about 10% more on average, but failure isn't the end
points.body: Using data tracking roughly 10 million entrepreneurship events since 2000, the authors found that founders' average income is about 10% higher than that of similar workers who didn't start a business — and that's before counting unrealized capital gains from selling the business, and the average already includes a large number of failures. About 20% of founders are serial entrepreneurs — it's the second or third venture that actually earns them yacht money. After a failure you can return to the labor market or start again and fix what went wrong last time.

points.h: Every congressional district has a millionaire business owner
points.body: The authors say "every congressional district has an everywhere millionaire." Unlike Silicon Valley and Wall Street, which are concentrated in specific geographic areas, almost every district has a car dealer. These business owners employ many people, pay a lot of sales tax, and are prominent in their local communities, which gives them outsized influence — their approval ratings are higher than those of the military, the Supreme Court, and Congress. About a quarter of members of Congress are private business owners; if you count law firm partners, that share can reach 40% to 50%. At the state and local level, because the positions are part-time and low-paid, business owners make up an even larger share — especially mayors.
